text: Every quantum computer you've read about is secretly a hybrid machine: a wall of ordinary classical electronics doing almost all of the physical work of generating, routing, and reading the signals that a much smaller number of qubits actually respond to. This lesson opens up that classical half of the stack.

This is what that classical half actually looks like — real control racks behind a quantum computer. None of this is quantum. All of it is decades-old electronics, just operated at extreme precision: generating a precisely shaped microwave pulse to rotate a qubit's state, or sending a probe signal in and capturing a very faint returning signal to read one out, without burying it in noise.

The core room-temperature components: arbitrary waveform generators, or AWGs, synthesize the baseband pulse shapes for each qubit operation. Microwave and RF signal generation mixes those shapes up to the qubit's actual operating frequency, typically several gigahertz, since the AWG alone usually can't generate that directly. DACs and ADCs convert between digital waveform data and the analog voltages the hardware needs, in both directions. And FPGAs sit in the loop to make real-time decisions — reading out a qubit mid-circuit and deciding, within microseconds, which pulse to apply next, a requirement for error correction and mid-circuit feedback.

Getting the chip cold is only half the problem — it has to be controlled from outside, and every line running into the cryostat is a potential heat leak. Attenuators at each stage reduce the signal's power and the thermal noise riding along with it. Filters strip out unwanted frequencies that could disturb the qubit. Amplifiers on the readout path boost an extremely weak return signal before it's lost in noise. Each qubit, in many current architectures, needs its own dedicated lines — so wiring density is a hard constraint on how many qubits a given fridge can support, and more wires means more heat load competing directly with keeping the chip cold enough to function.
Next lesson: what's actually inside the "gate" abstraction you've been using this whole course — underneath a Hadamard or a CNOT is nothing but a carefully shaped analog pulse.
